To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the distribution of polychorinated dibenzop-dioxins and furans (PCDD/FS) was examined according the particle size in marine sediment, with a particular emphasis on fine particulates; despite different size profiles and the PCDD/F content of the sediment at each location, the PCDD/F level of the fractions tends to rise as the particle size decreases; the PCDD/FS level in the finest particles was up to 16x higher than the coarsest particles and is related

the levels of polychlorodibenzo-p-dioxin and polychlorodibenzofurans increase with decreasing particle size, and that fine particulate matter (less than or equal to 10 microm) may be the most important fraction of marine sediments to consider for the risk assessment of polychlorobiphenyls, polychlorodioxins, and polychlorofurans.
the distribution of PCDD/F in marine sediments depends on the size of the particles, and the fine particles (less than 5 microm) are a major source of PCDD/F to the aquatic food chain.

the characterization of particle-bound PCDD/Fs, which is a key issue in the environmental risk assessment of marine sediments.
the characterization of PCDD/F levels and particle size distribution in sediments from different coastal sites.
the distribution of PCDD/F levels among particle fractions of marine sedi-ments, and the results will help to understand the fate and behavior of PCDD/F in the marine environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fine particles (<10 microm) in marine sediments are a major source of bioavailable PCDD/Fs.
the PCDD/Fs are concentrated in the finest particles, and the PCDD/F concentrations in the fine particulates are associated with organic carbon content.
the fine particle size fraction of the sediment is the main source of the PCDD/Fs to the aquatic ecosystem.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PCDD/Fs are strongly associated with fine particulates in marine sediments.
PCDD/Fs are more likely to be bioavailable in fine sediment particles, and that this may be a major pathway for PCDD/Fs to enter aquatic organisms and the human food chain.

PCDD/Fs are strongly associated with fine sediment particles, which are easily consumed by biota, and that the fine sediment fraction is a good indicator for PCDD/Fs and their bioavailability in the marine environment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PCDD/Fs are more abundant in the finer particle size fractions, which are the size range that can be consumed by benthic organisms.
PCDD/F concentrations in marine sediments are highly correlated with organic carbon content and are highest in fine particulates.
the PCDD/F content in the finest particles is a useful indicator of PCDD/F levels for the entire sediment.
